questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Complex Number in Polar Form
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ We get

$$
z=0+(-2)\text{i}.
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=0+(-2)\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(0)}^{2}+{(-2)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

      

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=0$  and $y=-2$ is negative, $z$ lies on the negative $y$-axis. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z=-2\text{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))
$$

questions.worked_solution:
In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $ represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\sqrt{3}>0$ and $y=-1<0,$ $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}| \\  & =2\pi -arctan\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6}))
$$

$$

$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{4})\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

     

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{1}{4}$ is positive and $y=-\frac{1}{4}$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-\frac{1}{4})}{(\frac{1}{4})}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z=\frac{1-\text{i}}{4}$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}))
$$

questions.problem:
Express $z=\frac{4}{1+\text{i}\sqrt{3}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $1-\text{i}\sqrt{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{4}{1+\text{i}\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{4(1-\text{i}\sqrt{3})}{(1+\text{i}\sqrt{3})(1-\text{i}\sqrt{3})} \\  & =\frac{4-4\text{i}\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}-{(\text{i}\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-4\text{i}\sqrt{3}}{1-(-3)} \\  & =\frac{4-4i\sqrt{3}}{4} \\  & =1-\sqrt{3}\,i\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=1-\sqrt{3}\,i,$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=1$ and $y=-\sqrt{3},$ $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=2\cdot \,(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}))
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{2}{1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-\text{i})}{(1+\text{i})(1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{2(1-\text{i})}{{1}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{2(1-\text{i})}{2} \\  & =1-\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=1$ is positive and $y=-1$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$

$$
z=\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}))

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{5}{4+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{{4}^{2}-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{16+9} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{25} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16+9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $ represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{4}{5}$ is positive and $y=-\frac{3}{5}$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-\frac{3}{5})}{(\frac{4}{5})}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ≈5.640,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

$$
z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5.640)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5.640)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{1-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{{1}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\,\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{9}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})).

questions.worked_solution:
To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

First, we find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the values and expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =18(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})) \\  & =18(-\frac{1}{2}+\text{i}\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{18}{2}+\text{i}\,\frac{18\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =-9+9\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\textrm{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\textrm{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $2+\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{(2-\text{i})(2+\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(2+\text{i}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}+\frac{3}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\textrm{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} .
$$

So, for $z= \dfrac{6}{5} +\dfrac{3}{5}\textrm{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36+9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{45}{25}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta$  represents the argument $\arg(z).$ Since $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$ and $y = \dfrac{3}{5}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(\frac{6}{5})}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =0.464,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z = \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{5} \left (\cos(0.464)+ \textrm{i} \sin(0.464) \right)
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Converting From Polar Form to Cartesian Form
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will simplify the right-hand side. Since $\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})) \\  & =4(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\text{i}\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}+2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$
